features.name: Caloris Planitia
features.description: One of the largest impact basins in the Solar System, stretching about 1,550 km across. Caloris formed when a massive impact shattered Mercury's crust and was later partly resurfaced by smooth volcanic plains.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Caloris is Latin for 'heat,' reflecting the basin's location near Mercury's hot equatorial region.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The shock from the Caloris impact likely converged on the opposite side of Mercury and helped create the planet's strange chaotic terrain.

features.name: Tolstoj
features.description: An ancient multi-ring impact basin roughly 390 km across, preserving some of Mercury's oldest visible crust. Its worn appearance makes it a key marker for the planet's early bombardment history.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Leo Tolstoy, the Russian novelist.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Tolstoj is so old that geologists use it to help define one of Mercury's earliest major geologic time periods.

features.name: Rembrandt
features.description: A spectacular 715 km wide impact basin with fractured floor material, smooth plains, and a broad ring structure. It is one of the younger large basins on Mercury and records both impact and volcanic resurfacing.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after the Dutch painter Rembrandt van Rijn.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Rembrandt was one of the standout discoveries of the MESSENGER mission because it had been hidden from Mariner 10's view.

features.name: Beethoven
features.description: A large, old impact basin about 640 km across with subdued rings and widespread smooth plains. It shows how later volcanism and impacts modified Mercury's giant early basins.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Ludwig van Beethoven, the German composer.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Beethoven was one of the major named basins already visible in the Mariner 10 era, long before Mercury was globally mapped.

features.name: Kuiper
features.description: A relatively young bright-rayed crater that stands out sharply against Mercury's darker surrounding terrain. Its freshness makes it a useful comparison point for younger impact processes on the planet.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Gerard Kuiper, a pioneering planetary scientist.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Kuiper is one of the easiest Mercurian craters to spot in global imagery because its bright rays look so fresh.

features.name: Raphael
features.description: One of Mercury's largest named craters, Raphael is a huge multi-ring impact structure whose broad floor and broken rim preserve the scale of the collisions that shaped the planet's older crust. It belongs with Shakespeare among the giant crater landmarks that make Mercury feel battered on a planetary scale.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Raphael, the Italian Renaissance painter.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Raphael is large enough that, in regional views, it reads less like a single crater and more like a major terrain province cut into Mercury's ancient surface.

features.name: Debussy
features.description: A striking bright-rayed crater in Mercury's southern hemisphere, Debussy stands out because its fresh ejecta streaks slash across much older terrain. It is one of the easiest impact features to pick out in the explorer when scanning east and south of Kuiper.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Claude Debussy, the French composer.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Debussy's extensive ray system makes it look geologically young compared with the darker, more muted crater fields around it.

features.name: Hiroshige
features.description: Hiroshige is a broad impact crater northeast of Debussy that reads clearly in regional views because of its size and preserved rim. It helps anchor the dense southern cratered terrain with another obvious named landmark near the Debussy-Kuiper region.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Utagawa Hiroshige, the Japanese artist.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Crater naming on Mercury turns regional exploration into a survey of major artists and composers, and Hiroshige is one of the names that stands out once you start using coordinates to hunt features.

features.name: Shakespeare
features.description: A large crater with a broad floor and pronounced rim, named under Mercury's convention of honoring artists, authors, and composers. It is part of the heavily cratered landscape that dominates much of the planet.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after William Shakespeare.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Mercury's crater naming theme means the map reads like a global roll call of major artists and writers.

features.name: Matisse
features.description: A well-preserved crater with central peaks and textured ejecta, representing the medium-size impact structures that pepper Mercury's ancient crust. Features like Matisse help compare Mercurian crater morphology with the Moon.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after Henri Matisse, the French artist.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Because Mercury and the Moon are both airless worlds, craters like Matisse are useful for direct cross-planet comparison.

features.name: Discovery Rupes
features.description: One of Mercury's giant lobate scarps, a cliff-like thrust fault created as the planet cooled and contracted. These scarps are among the clearest signs that Mercury shrank as its interior lost heat.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after HMS Discovery, continuing Mercury's rupes convention of honoring ships of exploration.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Mercury's scarps show that the whole planet actually got smaller over time as it cooled.

features.name: Hero Rupes
features.description: A long cliff-like scarp that cuts across older terrain, recording tectonic compression as Mercury's crust adjusted to planetary cooling. Features like Hero Rupes reveal that Mercury remained tectonically active after its heaviest bombardment era.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Named after HMS Hero, following Mercury's ship-naming rule for rupes features.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Some Mercurian scarps are hundreds of kilometers long, making them enormous cliffs on a planet only slightly larger than Earth's Moon.

features.name: Pantheon Fossae
features.description: A striking web of radial troughs near the center of Caloris Basin, often compared to spokes spreading from a wheel hub. The feature likely formed as the basin floor was uplifted, fractured, and modified by volcanism and tectonics.

details.label: Origin of Name
details.value: Pantheon is named after the famous domed temple in Rome.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Pantheon Fossae is sometimes nicknamed 'the Spider' because its radial fractures look like legs spreading out across Caloris.

features.name: Northern Smooth Plains
features.description: A vast expanse of relatively smooth terrain interpreted as ancient flood volcanism. These plains indicate Mercury experienced major episodes of lava flooding, not just impact cratering.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The northern smooth plains were one of the strongest pieces of evidence that Mercury had major volcanic resurfacing, not only impact-driven geology.

features.name: Mercury North Pole
features.description: Mercury's north polar region contains permanently shadowed crater floors that never see direct sunlight. Radar and spacecraft data show these cold traps likely preserve water ice despite Mercury's intense proximity to the Sun.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Even on the innermost planet, some crater floors are cold enough to hide water ice for long periods.

features.name: Mercury South Pole
features.description: The south polar region also hosts permanently shadowed craters that are strong candidates for water-ice deposits. These polar cold traps are among Mercury's most surprising discoveries.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Mercury's poles are a reminder that temperature on an airless world can depend more on sunlight geometry than distance from the Sun.
